eid_al_adha.intro: Eid al-Adha, the Feast of the Sacrifice, is Egypt's longest religious holiday with four days off. It falls at the end of the pilgrimage to Mecca and commemorates Abraham's readiness to sacrifice his son.
eid_al_adha.history: Muslims have celebrated the feast since the seventh century. In Egypt it absorbed older customs of the Nile valley, and under the Mamluks and Ottomans Cairo's sultans distributed meat to the poor in huge public feasts.
eid_al_adha.traditions: Families sacrifice a sheep or share a calf and give a third of the meat to the poor. The classic dish is fattah, rice and bread soaked in garlic-vinegar broth topped with meat. Egyptians bake kahk, sugar-dusted butter cookies, visit relatives and take children to parks and the zoo.
funFacts: Egyptians call it the Big Feast, Eid el-Kebir, and Eid al-Fitr the Small Feast.
Cairo's butchers work through the night before the feast.
Children receive eidiya, small gifts of money, from every relative they visit.
The Nile corniche and the pyramids are packed with families on the feast days.

islamic_new_year.intro: The Islamic New Year on 1 Muharram marks the start of the Hijri calendar and is a quiet public holiday in Egypt. It commemorates the Prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622.
islamic_new_year.history: Caliph Umar established the Hijri calendar in 638, counting the years from the Hijra, the migration to Medina. Because the year has twelve lunar months and only 354 days, the New Year moves about eleven days earlier each Gregorian year.
islamic_new_year.traditions: The day is marked with prayers and reflection rather than parties. Families enjoy the day off together, and the government announces the holiday date only after the new moon is sighted. Ten days later Egyptians eat the sweet wheat pudding called Ashura.
funFacts: The Hijri year 1448 begins in June 2026.
Egypt uses the Hijri calendar for religious holidays and the Gregorian for everything else.
Ashura pudding is made with wheat, milk, sugar and nuts and shared with neighbours.
Many Egyptians simply use the day for a long weekend, since there are no fixed rituals.

prophet_muhammads_birthday.intro: Mawlid al-Nabi on 12 Rabi al-Awwal celebrates the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad. Egypt celebrates it more colourfully than almost any other country, with sweets, processions and Sufi gatherings.
prophet_muhammads_birthday.history: The Fatimid caliphs in Cairo were the first to celebrate the Prophet's birthday publicly in the tenth century. The traditions of sugar dolls and mounted knights made of candy go back to those Fatimid parades and have survived for a thousand years.
prophet_muhammads_birthday.traditions: Shops fill with halawet el-mawlid, sweets made of nuts, sesame and sugar, and with the sugar doll arouset el-mawlid that grooms give to their brides. Sufi orders hold processions and chanting nights around the mosques of al-Hussein and Sayyida Zaynab in Cairo.
funFacts: The sugar doll is said to represent a Fatimid caliph's wife who joined the parade in a white dress.
Egyptians buy an estimated 50,000 tonnes of mawlid sweets every year.
Al-Azhar mosque holds a special celebration on the eve.
The date is set by the Hijri calendar and moves each year.

sinai_liberation_day.intro: Sinai Liberation Day on 25 April celebrates the return of the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt in 1982, after fifteen years of Israeli occupation following the Six-Day War.
sinai_liberation_day.history: Israel captured Sinai in 1967. The October War of 1973, the Camp David Accords of 1978 and the peace treaty of 1979 led to a phased withdrawal, and on 25 April 1982 the last Israeli troops left. Taba, the final strip, was returned by arbitration in 1989.
sinai_liberation_day.traditions: The President lays wreaths and awards medals to veterans, and celebrations take place in Sharm el-Sheikh, El-Arish and other Sinai towns with concerts, flags and fireworks. Schools stage patriotic performances in the days before.
funFacts: Sinai is Egypt's only Asian territory, making the country transcontinental.
The peninsula holds Mount Sinai, where tradition says Moses received the Ten Commandments.
Taba, only one square kilometre, took seven more years of negotiation.
Sharm el-Sheikh has grown from a fishing village into a resort city since the liberation.

revolution_day.intro: Revolution Day on 23 July commemorates the 1952 revolution of the Free Officers that ended the monarchy and founded the Egyptian republic. It is the country's traditional national day.
revolution_day.history: On 23 July 1952 a group of army officers led by Gamal Abdel Nasser and Muhammad Naguib seized power. King Farouk abdicated three days later, and Egypt was declared a republic in 1953. Nasser went on to nationalise the Suez Canal and shape the Arab world for two decades.
revolution_day.traditions: The President gives a televised address, military and civilian medals are awarded and state television broadcasts documentaries about the revolution. Families enjoy the day off in the summer heat, often at the coast in Alexandria.
funFacts: King Farouk sailed into exile on his yacht from Alexandria on 26 July 1952.
Nasser was only 34 years old when the officers took power.
The revolution's six principles are still quoted in Egyptian school books.
Egypt's current flag is derived from the Arab Liberation flag of 1952.

june_30_revolution.intro: The 30 June holiday commemorates the mass protests of 2013 against President Mohamed Morsi, which led to his removal by the army three days later. It has been a public holiday since 2014.
june_30_revolution.history: One year after Morsi took office, millions of Egyptians demonstrated across the country on 30 June 2013. The armed forces removed him on 3 July, suspended the constitution and appointed an interim government; Abdel Fattah el-Sisi was elected president in 2014.
june_30_revolution.traditions: The day is marked by official speeches, patriotic broadcasts and events at Tahrir Square and the presidential palace. For most Egyptians it is a mid-summer day off spent with family or at the beach.
funFacts: The protests were organised by a petition campaign called Tamarod, meaning rebellion.
It is one of two revolution anniversaries in Egypt's calendar, with 25 January.
The holiday falls in the hottest part of the Egyptian summer.
The events remain politically sensitive and are described differently by different groups.

armed_forces_day.intro: Armed Forces Day on 6 October commemorates the crossing of the Suez Canal in the October War of 1973, when Egyptian troops broke through the Bar Lev Line on the first day of the war.
armed_forces_day.history: On 6 October 1973 Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on Israeli positions in Sinai and the Golan Heights. The crossing of the canal was a major military achievement and led, six years later, to the peace treaty and the return of Sinai.
armed_forces_day.traditions: The President attends a military ceremony, wreaths are laid at the Unknown Soldier memorial and the 6 October Panorama in Cairo shows the crossing. The satellite city 6th of October near Cairo is named after the day, and the Suez Canal towns hold celebrations.
funFacts: Egyptian engineers used water cannons to breach the sand wall of the Bar Lev Line.
President Sadat was assassinated during the anniversary parade in 1981.
The 6th of October Bridge in Cairo is one of the longest in Africa.
The war began on Yom Kippur, which is why Israel calls it the Yom Kippur War.

revolution_day_2011_national_police_day.intro: The 25 January holiday combines Police Day, which honours the 1952 battle of Ismailia, with the anniversary of the 2011 revolution that began with mass protests on the same date.
revolution_day_2011_national_police_day.history: On 25 January 1952 Egyptian policemen in Ismailia refused to surrender to British forces and fought until about fifty of them were killed. In 2011 protesters chose the same day to march against the Mubarak government; eighteen days later the president resigned.
revolution_day_2011_national_police_day.traditions: The President honours police officers and the families of those killed, and state media broadcast programmes about both events. Public celebrations are modest, and many Egyptians use the day for a winter outing.
funFacts: Police Day only became a public holiday in 2009, two years before the revolution.
Tahrir Square, the centre of the 2011 protests, means Liberation Square.
The 2011 protests lasted eighteen days.
The battle of Ismailia is also remembered by a police museum in the city.

easter_monday_eg.intro: Sham El-Nessim, celebrated on the Monday after Coptic Easter, is Egypt's ancient spring festival. It is shared by Muslims and Christians alike and is one of the oldest continuously celebrated holidays in the world.
easter_monday_eg.history: The festival dates back to the harvest celebration of Shemu in pharaonic times, more than 4,500 years ago. Its name means "smelling the breeze" and comes from the ancient Egyptian word for the season. When Egypt became Christian the date was tied to Easter, and it survived the arrival of Islam unchanged.
easter_monday_eg.traditions: Families picnic in parks, along the Nile and in the countryside from early morning. The traditional foods are feseekh, a salted fermented mullet, coloured eggs, green onions, lettuce and lupin beans. Eggs are painted with wishes and the family brings them outdoors at dawn.
funFacts: The painted eggs of Sham El-Nessim may be the origin of Easter eggs.
Feseekh is so strongly flavoured that health officials warn about it every year.
The festival falls on the same day for the whole country regardless of religion.
Ancient Egyptians believed spring onions warded off evil spirits.
